utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Judge Mindua can't take part in today's hearing due to another urgent appointment. Therefore the Chamber decided to sit only with two Judges pursuant to Rule 15 bis. I think the next witness should be brought in, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you, good morning to Your Honour, and good morning everyone. Mr. President, I would ask, as was the case yesterday, for the witness to be provided with a caution pursuant to Rule 90(E). I think it's appropriate in the circumstances as it was yesterday and that's the only preliminary issue I wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- the affirmation to tell the truth which is shown to you on the card now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And please sit down. I assume that it is not the first time that you are testifying in this Tribunal. You know the rules and the procedure, and I would like to let you know that you have, as a witness, certain rights. You have the Rule 90(E) of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence and I would like to read the text to you so that you are aware of your rights. I quote: "The witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." This is the paragraph in our Rules. Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now Mr. Vanderpuye has some questions for you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You recall we met yesterday morning and I'm going to ask you a few questions in relation to your evidence today. The first thing I want to ask you is: Do you recall having testified in the case of Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al. on 26 June 2007?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was your testimony truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was truthful and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to review your testimony before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you read it or did you listen to it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I listened to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And having listened to your testimony, does it fairly and accurately reflect what you would say if you were asked -- if you were examined today and asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I would tender the witness's previous testimony, which is P1102.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As well as the attendant exhibits in that testimony which are P1103 and P1104.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have a brief summary of the witness's prior testimony, and then I have a few questions for him. Mr. Milosevic was born in 1964 in Lupoglav, Kladanj municipality in Bosnia. He fulfilled his compulsory JNA military service in 1983 in Sarajevo. He joined the Army of Republika Srpska in May or June of 1992 and served until September 1994 when he was demobilised. In March or April 1995, Mr. Milosevic was remobilised and sent to the 6th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade as the deputy commander of that battalion under battalion commander Ostoja Stanisic. Between 10 a.m. and 12 noon on the morning of 14 July 1995, Milosevic was at the 6th Battalion command in the village of Petkovci when he was contacted by the Zvornik Brigade duty officer and informed that in around two hours a group of Muslim prisoners would be transferred, accompanied by security, to the Petkovci elementary school. When Mr. Milosevic's commander Ostoja Stanisic returned to the battalion command around 2 hours later, Milosevic informed him of the call from the Zvornik Brigade duty officer. That same afternoon, Stanisic received a call from the Zvornik Brigade duty officer. Following the call, around 1600 or 1700 hours that afternoon, Stanisic instructed Milosevic to look for Beara near the Petkovci elementary school and convey a message to him to report to the brigade command. Milosevic went towards the Petkovci elementary school. He met Zvornik Brigade assistant commander for security, Drago Nikolic at a crossroads leading to the school. Drago Nikolic pointed out Beara to Milosevic and Milosevic conveyed the message to Beara to contact the brigade. Milosevic saw four or five military policemen with Nikolic and Beara and uniformed troops guarding the school. He also saw a few lorries and buses parked further down the road, and a blue Golf III car. Milosevic then returned to the battalion and reported to his commander, Ostoja Stanisic, that he had relayed the message to Beara. Stanisic then conveyed this information to the brigade. Milosevic heard isolated shots and bursts of gun-fire coming from the direction of the school late that afternoon. He stated that he did not investigate and that he did not pass the school again that day. Although he spent the night of 15 July at the battalion command, Milosevic said that he did not learn that the Muslim prisoners at Petkovci school had been killed until around 20 July, after he had been wounded and placed in hospital. That concludes my summary, Your Honours. I do have a few additional questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, prior to serving as the deputy commander of the 6th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade in 1995, Mr. Milosevic, did you serve in any other positions as a member of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I served in other positions in the VRS, specifically in the Zvornik Brigade. In 1993, I was the assistant commander for morale. And in 1994, I was the assistant commander for security in the battalion. I'm not sure if it was the 3rd or the 1st Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in 1994 when you were -- first let me ask you, you said that you were not sure if it was the 1st or the 3rd Battalion. Would it refresh your --

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which battalion it was, but I was the assistant commander for security in this battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I would just remind you that in your Blagojevic testimony at page 5639, and that would be lines 20 through 23 of that transcript, you indicated that you served in the 1st Battalion as the assistant commander for security for about six or seven months. Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does refresh my recollection and it was like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you've indicated that that was within the Zvornik Brigade. Did you have contacts with the chief of security for the Zvornik Brigade during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the period while I was serving in this duty, we had contacts with the chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade, Mr. Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this is the same Drago Nikolic that you've indicated in your previous testimony as the person that pointed out Beara to you near the Petkovci school on 14 July 1995, that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And at that time did you know who Beara was?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't know who Beara was. It was the first time I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of your relationship with Nikolic, was it such that it would give you cause to believe or give you pause, with a p, in respect of his pointing out Beara to you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is there any reason that you have to believe that Mr. Nikolic would have misled you as to who Beara was when you asked him?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to show you a couple of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The first will be P1103.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a -- it's an aerial image that you marked in your last testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, this is just fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you could just tell us briefly what this shows and then I'll show you another exhibit. You don't have to mark it, you can just tell us what it's supposed to indicate.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We can see that the road from the battalion command to the crossroads where I met Drago Nikolic is marked in a red line, and to the left where the primary school is, it's the plateau with the primary school. It's marked also in red.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to show you the next part of this exhibit -- well, another exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's P1104.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you briefly just tell us what this is intended to show, what the X is and then what the red line is?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's the old school and the red line marks the road from the new school to the battalion school, or rather, the old school where the command of the 6th Battalion was accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you P1091. I believe it's the aerial image from which those two marked photos were taken -- was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you are able to find your bearings on this, this one I'd like you to mark, just to show what the other two images reflect. So if you could just show the starting point, the meeting point, and the school on this one, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the old school or the new one?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you can see the elementary school, if you could mark it that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could mark the point, the intersection or near the intersection where you met Drago Nikolic and Beara?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if you can show where the command of the 6th Battalion is situated. Maybe we'll mark these 1, 2, and 3 respectively so that it's clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This aerial photograph with markings will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The red markings, Your Honours, on Exhibit P1091 made in red by this witness would be assigned Exhibit P01138.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you 65 ter 1464, which is also a map. Okay. If we can zoom in to, you see the number 6 in there, if you can focus in on that and you'll see a flag marked with the number 6 as well. It's right in the middle of the screen, just about. We can get a little bit bigger. And if you can zoom in right there on the flag, that would be helpful. Okay, I think that's pretty good.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, are you able to recognise the location that's indicated -- well, the location, there are many, but the location where you see a 6 with a flag in it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Baljkovica, Petkovci, that's where the command of the 6th Battalion was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to -- if we can have the flag move a little towards the centre of the screen, that would be helpful. A little bit down. Okay. That's just fine. Maybe we can blow it up also. Great.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like you to mark this one, this map as well, but first let me ask you, where the flag is depicted in this map, is that accurate as to where the 6th Battalion command was actually situated?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, the circle, it's a populated place, and it was approximately there, now whether it's exact or not, but I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Because the battalion command was here where the populated place is, that is Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. That's good to know. Now, where the triangle is at the base of that flag with the number 6 in it, that would be Petkovci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And about -- do you see the -- do you see the water to the right of that flag? There's some distance away, and you can see a body of water there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us where the dam is located relative to where the command of the 6th Battalion is, and if you could mark it, that would be helpful, if you are able.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The dam was in the populated place called Djulici, and I suppose that it is this up here, as I was living in was in Lupe for ten years and from the place where I lived you could see the dam. Am I supposed to mark it, but how? With an X or --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With a B for Brana, I think. That would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us about how far the dam is from the battalion command, the 6th Battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, but as Djulici were 2, 2 and a half or 3 kilometres away and so were Lupe, that means that the dam would have to be around 2 and a half to 3 kilometres from the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like it to tender this exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That marked map will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the markings made by this witness in red on 65 ter 01464 will be assigned P01139.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I just have a few questions more for you. As the former assistant commander for security at the battalion level, who were you -- to whom were you subordinated, back in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In 1994, well, I was subordinated to the commander of my battalion and I also co-operated with Mr. Drago Nikolic who was the assistant commander for security of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of your relationship with the security structures of the brigade, can you tell us what that was, what was your responsibility toward the higher security organs?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will tell you what I was doing at the time and how I understood my duties as the assistant commander for security in the battalion, in relation to the chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade Drago Nikolic. It all came down to several operational tasks. Essentially that we should be in contact so that we would say whether the line or the zone of responsibility was secure, that was the zone and the line of our brigade and our battalion. And if necessary, we would inform the command of the Zvornik Brigade about intelligence, that is to say, the movements of enemy forces in front of our line and our defence sector. What I can say is that we spent most time by co-operating with the military police of all the security structures at the brigade level because very often it happens to us when there was rotation of troops at the line, that the line was not filled, and then company commanders requested that the soldiers be transported to our lines and we requested the brigade command and the military police, which was controlled by the security, to bring in these men and transport them to the lines so that the line would be secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you in your capacity as assistant commander for security at the battalion level receive orders from your commander, that is the battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you receive orders from Drago Nikolic as your superior along the security chain of communication?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Drago Nikolic, as far as security is concerned and as far as I can remember, and this was a peaceful time where there weren't many combat operations, from time to time as required we would report, I can't tell you the exact number, how many times, but we would report and Drago Nikolic as the assistant commander for security would issue certain guide-lines and instructions and as to how we were to work. For the most part it had to do with potential movements of Muslim forces in front of our lines where our battalion covered and they would indicate this to us so we would be prepared so that we wouldn't be caught by surprise by the enemy. So for the most part that is what it boiled down to. And there was also certain co-ordination with the military police in terms of securing the defence line, mainly to do with reinforcements and bringing in fresh men to fill in the gaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was it part of your responsibility as the assistant commander for security at the battalion level, was it part of your responsibility to undertake certain measures to detect and arrest perpetrators in respect of criminal acts within the area of responsibility or within the area of -- rather, within the area of responsibility for the security organs generally and for the battalion particularly?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you at any time involved in either gathering information or undertaking any criminal proceedings against perpetrators of criminal acts during the time that you were assistant commander for security at the battalion level?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all I can say is that there was an incident sometime in 1994, I believe in spring-time, but I'm not sure, and this was while I was the assistant commander for security, where one of our companies captured a member of the Muslim Army who was drunk and he just happened to run into our lines. He was held at the battalion. He was questioned briefly. We asked him what his name was and what unit he belonged to, and we informed of this the brigade command and asked them to send military -- the military police to take over the prisoner and escort him to the brigade. That's how it happened. The military police did come. They took in Muslim to the brigade, and as far as I know, this same person was later on exchanged and returned to his territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And would the questioning of a prisoner such as this one that you've described, would that be within the remit of your responsibilities as a security officer at the battalion level?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, as I said that I was a member of the Army of Republika Srpska and that I was where I was, but I wasn't very familiar with the exact duties of either the assistant commander of the battalion or the battalion because I never went to any military school, so I just felt that it was my duty to inform the brigade if someone was captured so that they could jot down the information. But as for the questioning itself and how that should be done, I did not go into that. There was no need for that and there were other people who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You know based upon your experience having been an assistant commander for security at the battalion level, do you know if it is within the responsibilities of a security officer such as yourself to question prisoners, whether it is within the responsibilities of that position to undertake measures to detect and arrest perpetrators of criminal acts, and whether it is within the responsibilities for that position to gather information about those criminal acts that can be used for conducting criminal proceedings? Is that your understanding of what your responsibilities, among other things, would entail?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that, in my view, and as far as I knew about the army and the command system in the army, I know that it was my duty as a security officer in the battalion to gather information on any movements of Muslims out in front of our defence line, to make sure that the line is secure and fully manned and to contact the brigade with any issues that -- with the military police. But as far as the criminal offences were concerned, I did not -- I was not aware that it was my duty, nor did I read any regulations to that effect so I couldn't really answer that question very accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, thank you very much for that candid response.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That concludes my direct examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Tolimir, please start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May there be peace unto this house and may God's will be done in these proceedings. And may the outcome be as God wishes and not as I wish, including today. I wish Mr. Milosevic a pleasant stay in The Hague and I wish to greet him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have a few questions for you about some matters that you testified earlier on because all of those transcripts were also admitted as evidence in these proceedings. And I would appreciate your patience, listen carefully to my questions, and please do try to make a brief pause after my question so that the interpreters can follow.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the Popovic transcript on page 1329, lines 3, 4 and 5, you said the following, and I will quote because neither you nor I can speak any English: "Before the war broke out in the former Yugoslavia" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And for the record, this is P1102.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Transcript page 13298. Lines 4 and 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Before the war broke out in the former Yugoslavia, I did not have a job. I was in Kladanj waiting to be employed at the bureau for employment." My question for you is this: How old were you before the war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before the war I was 27 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, please, based on what Mr. Vanderpuye read, your resume, you said that you were born in Kladanj. Were your parents too born in Kladanj? In other words, do you hail from that area?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was born in Lupoglav village, and it was in Kladanj municipality, and that's where I was born, my parents were born, as well as our forbearers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, the Lupoglav village is your ancient home, as we would put it in our language?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Popovic transcript you said that your mother remained in Lupoglav for awhile, and you also said: "Not only my mother," and I quote, "some 50 people or so stayed in the village and they were all arrested and taken to a camp in Stupari, in Kladanj municipality, where they were held until July 1993 when they were exchanged under the auspices of the Red Cross. This exchange was in Bijeljina." My question is this: How long was your mother held in detention, because it doesn't say so here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In late May and early June 1992, and at this time I worked in Sekovici already, some inhabitants of my village, Lupoglav, had already been evacuated to Sekovici, and a larger number of them, including my mother, her brothers and other relations, remained in the village and were captured by the Muslim forces, which at the time was the Kladanj Territorial Defence. And from the village they were taken by force to Stupari to a camp which was housed across -- in a building across from the school, and they were held there until July 1993, I believe, when they were exchanged through the mediation of the International Red Cross and the exchange took place in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My apologies, I really wanted to ask you when they were captured, if you can recall, whether it was the same month or the same year? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were captured in 1992 in early June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what happened with their property? Did anyone stay back? Did any inhabitants of Serb ethnicities remain in the village?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as the property is concerned in my village, Lupoglav, all of the properties were then devastated. They were looted and burnt down. In other words, nothing was left of the village. It was razed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any of those individuals whose properties had been burnt down, did any of them take part in any combat operations or were they another category?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all these were unarmed civilians and elderly people, so that not one of them ever took part in any combat operations nor were there any combat operations in May and June 1992 at the time when they were captured and taken to the Stupari camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us please, other than your village, were there any other villages and places in Kladanj municipality that you know of where people had been -- people of Serb ethnicities had been removed in a similar manner? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in view of the fact that I spent my entire life there, my career, I worked there, I knew most of the people there, and I believe and I think that all of the villages in Kladanj municipality, and I'm talking about June 1992, all these villages were torched and all the people who stayed behind, who hadn't been evacuated earlier on, were captured and taken to Stupari. So that camp was a detention camp not only for this village but also from some other villages.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the names of these villages. The interpreters didn't catch the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said my village Lupoglav, Matijevici, Olovci, Brdijeli, Obrcevac, Vranovici, Mladovo, Pelemisi, I'm not sure about Pelemisi, the entire area, but part of it, and other Serb villages which were connected with Olovo which I was not aware of at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, again we see that not all of the villages were recorded in the transcript and I would ask the witness to repeat the names again and just tell us whether they had the same fate as Lupoglav, whether they were looted, torched and so on, and the people taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the system with recording is the following. If you seen the signs between Olovci and Vranovici, that means it will be checked later and compared with the tape. You can be sure that will be corrected and added, so there is no need to repeat it again. But if the interpreters tell us that they didn't catch it, they couldn't translate it and therefore I asked for repetition. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So, Witness, would you just answer my new question, in other words, were these villages too devastated, as you said, and how? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, all of these villages, all the villages that were inhabited by Serbs were torched and demolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 1329 -- 13299 of the transcript, in the Popovic transcript, you talked about your promotion while you were with the Army of Republika Srpska. You spoke about this in lines 5 through 8. I won't reiterate any of what you said there, but could you just tell us here whether you have ever completed any kind of military school? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in the Republika Srpska army I was on various functions. As I said, I was assistant commander for security and then for morale, and then in the end I was the deputy commander of the 6th Battalion. My rank was that of corporal and I was conferred this rank when I was in the Yugoslav Army still and I did not -- I did not get promoted at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, the reason I put this question to you was to show that when you did not answer some of the Prosecutor's questions, it was not because you weren't willing to but because you didn't have the appropriate background.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did not -- I was not trained as an officer and I was not very familiar with what which functions entailed. I did the best I knew how.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you actually complete the course as assistant commander for security? Did you complete the course for that position?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you complete the course for assistant commander for morale? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The position of assistant commander, does that mean that the person in charge is the commander whereas you were just his assistant at the battalion level, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My apologies. Within the scope of the duties that you carried out and that you took over from the person who was there before you, did you just carry out those duties for the period that you were appointed to that position, say six months, and then you were transferred to something else, you would do something else?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't go through any kind of training. We just carried out the take-over and we would be assigned to various duties within the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your battalion commander know what the tasks and duties of the position for which you were the assistant were?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does that mean that you could not lie to him or deceive him as to what it was that you were doing or were suppose today do because he knew very well what your duties as assistant commander for security entailed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell us now whether at any point in time you were taken to task because of the work that you did in the course of your duties, or were you ever commended for your work, and were these commendations relayed to you directly or via the brigade commander and whether they were done in public in front of all the other members of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that, as far as I can recall, I never received any commendations either at the brigade command or elsewhere. I did my job to the best of my abilities, but I was never commended for my work, nor was I ever promoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell the Trial Chamber whether all assistant commanders in the battalion such as yours have to carry out the tasks as set forth by the commander?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've already are said, I was the assistant commander for security. I was one of the assistants as a morale person, and of course I obeyed the orders issued by my commander. That was crucial. And as for the rules and the structure of the chain of command, I really didn't learn -- I didn't read anything about it, so I don't really know much about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, tell me, please, can a subordinate change orders issued by his commander? In other words -- or to put it more clearly, did the commander issue orders that had to be followed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. General, my apologies, but could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did commanders issue written or oral orders for combat operations and activities related to that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you carrying out your duties at the location which were pointed out by the Prosecutor a little earlier?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The battalion forces, were they deployed there pursuant to an order or were they there just on their own decision? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I will repeat again. As far as the command structure is concerned, I wouldn't really go into that much, but I assumed that they were deployed there pursuant to an order and that it was known where a battalion or a company was that was part of that battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As an assistant commander, were you allowed to alter any orders issued by the commander? Were you allowed to say, Well, we want -- we will not defend that feature or that hill but some other? Were there such instances where a subordinate commander would take his own or make his own -- issue his own commands?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't mean to interrupt the cross-examination, but the question seems a bit confusing because not clear as to what period of time we are talking about. If we are talking about 1995, then the record is clear that the position of this witness at that time was the deputy commander of the 6th Battalion. And it's unclear whether we are talking about his position as a deputy commander or as an assistant commander, which are completely different, completely different functions. And I'm sure Mr. Tolimir wants to make that point as well, but I think it's important to be clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, that will be helpful indeed if you could make clear if your specific question is related to 1995 or another period of time. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked about 1995 and I mentioned the place where the Prosecutor showed the flag and I asked you whether you were there. But let me ask you again, while you were in the 6th Battalion, could you ever change the position of the battalion commander about positioning the defence forces or any other decision in the zone where combat activities were being carried out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As my duty in the battalion was assistant commander, that is to say, deputy commander of the battalion, I could not change anything that the commander had ordered. I had to obey the commander just like anyone else within the battalion command, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you change the commander's decision relating to security? When he would say, Well, the security will have to do this and that, could you change this decision or did you have to obey the order? What I have in mind is the period while you were the assistant for security in the battalion, those six months.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think that as the assistant commander for security I was not supposed to change any decisions. We just obeyed our commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the commander issue all security tasks to you as you were the one who had to carry out these decisions and implement them in the field? Did he regulate that by written orders or by something that he would convey to you orally? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I already said earlier and let me repeat now, as assistant commanders for security within the battalion, we had some contacts with the assistant commander for security in the brigade in the sense that we would have possible briefings, and it all came down to determining whether the line was secure. In other words, whether any movements had been noticed or any attempts to break through the forward defence line of the battalion, and what I already said, we co-operated with the military police in the sense of filling up positions along the line so as to make sure that it would be secure. So we obeyed the commander, but we also had some contacts with the security commander of the brigade, specifically in connection with the issues that I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You probably meant the assistant commander for security because there's no commander for security?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I meant the assistant commander for security in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could he issue orders to you, I mean the assistant commander for security in the brigade, orders that would be contrary to the orders and tasks that had been issued to the battalion and that were supposed to be implemented in the field? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can only speak for myself. We did not have any specific orders that we would receive from the assistant commander of the Zvornik Brigade. The meetings came down to the security of the line and in any case, it's probable, although I cannot confirm this, that the assistant commander had some contacts with battalion commanders. In any case, as the deputy commander of the battalion, I had to obey the orders of the battalion commander. And let me repeat once again, we did have some contacts with the assistant commander from the brigade for security, and that was Mr. Drago Nikolic in this case, because during these seven or eight months I held this position -- but fortunately it was more or less a peaceful period so there wasn't much need for any additional orders or whatever else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you this and I made an error in my question on purpose, but you answered as it was. I asked you whether this assistant commander could issue any orders, but an assistant cannot issue orders because it's logical that the commander should issue them, your commander should issue orders to you just as you said, and his commander would issue orders to him on the basis of his proposal. Did you possibly have the chance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think everybody knows what my objection will be, which is the lead-in to the question. I just want to clarify once again whether or not this is a position that the Defence is taking for the purposes of representing the Defence position in the case because I know that at the beginning of the case, Mr. Tolimir was advised with respect to statements of fact that he may make as an accused in this case, and I see that in this particular instance he has made certain representations concerning the manner in which orders are conveyed either by assistant commanders or commanders, not in the context of a question but separate and apart from any question. And I want to be sure of two things. One is that he is aware of his right with respect to making factual representations as an accused in this case. And two, whether or not it is his position or whether or not he is representing the Defence position in making these kinds of representations for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think everybody who's listening realised that the last question was not a question but a statement. That is absolutely true, and we have had some instances of a similar kind in the past. You should be very careful with that, Mr. Tolimir, and you should put questions to the witness and not make any statements. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I just explained to the witness why I asked him an erroneous question because Mr. Vanderpuye asked him the question and he answered the way he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I understand you. You would always like to explain why you put the question, but in the proper examination it is never necessary to give a reason for certain kind of a question. This is up to you. Nobody wants to know that. You should make your cross-examination. There is no need for any reasoning. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please tell the Trial Chamber whether you could give any tasks to those who were not members of your battalion but were members of the army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, I was the deputy commander of the 6th Battalion. I never issued any orders or gave any tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us did you ever carry out a task or an order that was contrary to how you understood morality or immorality or whether something was right or wrong or how much you knew about the customs and laws that were in force at the period?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, can you please repeat the question, it was a longish one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. I'll shorten it. Did you ever carry out an order which you believed was not right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you ever issued such an order by your battalion commander or the brigade commander? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who could give orders to you in this chain of command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I already said, I was the deputy battalion commander and I only obeyed the orders of my battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move to a different group of questions now because you stated clearly what you could and should be doing during these six months. On page 13307 of the transcript in the Popovic case, lines 24 and 25, and 13308, lines 1 to 8, you stated the following, I will quote: "In the morning on the 15th of July, early in the morning, my commander, Ostoja Stanisic, sent me once again to the defence sector of the 4th Company in our battalion because we had received information that during the night, or in the late -- in the early evening, that two of the trenches had been abandoned or, rather, that they had been hit by a hand-held launcher and the troops had withdrawn to the left and to the right of this trench and thus left an empty space in our line. So on the orders of my commander, I went there" -- my commander, I'm sorry, I didn't say the word "my commander." "I went there with two or three soldiers to see what had happened and what needed to be done in order to re-establish the line so that we wouldn't have any breaches in the line." Thank you. Did I quote correctly what you said about what was happening at the time and does that correspond to your description?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it happened that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: For the record, just tell us which troops withdrew to the left or the right of the trenches which were now empty? Just so that it would be clear for the record, it's not clear whether these were our troops or troops of another army and so on?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Two trenches that were part of the 4th Company of the 6th Battalion, these were the trenches. The 4th Company of the 6th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade, two of these trenches had been abandoned because in the late evening, the two trenches had been hit from hand-held launchers and these troops had moved to adjacent trenches. And this part of the line had become empty and was not secured anymore. This is why I went up there so that we would try to cover that so that we wouldn't have any problems and have enemy soldiers move through the gap, come to us from behind and wreak havoc among our troops the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell us, who was it that broke through these two trenches? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The shells were fired from Muslim positions from a hand-held launcher of the Muslim Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it from the forward line or from the depth of the territory? Could you estimate that at the site when you were assessing the situation? What did the soldiers tell you where did the fire come from, because a hand-held launcher is used in close combat?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, as it was a hand-held launcher, it was close contact. It means that they were close to the positions of our defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to answer my question completely, did they come over from the front or did they come from the depth of the territory, these shells that were fired against your positions?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember the date on which this happened? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was during the late hours on the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And you went there, as we know, on the 15th of July; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 15th of July early in the morning I went to the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you now please tell us what were the combat activities on the 15th of July in the zone or defence sector of your battalion? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 15th of July, as far as I remember, there was some fire against our positions from the Muslim forces from the sector of Nezuk and Zaseok. And as for our line, I have to say that at the time our line was weakened in terms of troops. We did not have a sufficient number of men to have the line stable, secure, and solid because many of the soldiers had been in the field and had not returned to the battalion yet at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you resolve this issue and how did you implement the order that your commander issued to you once the line had been broken through and once the VRS soldiers had abandoned their positions on the line?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, some of the troops were sent from the rear of the battalion in order to temporarily fill in this gap.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any combat going on on the 15th, 16th and 17th of July, and if so, can you please describe what sort of combat it was?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of July, 1995, in the evening, as far as I can remember, the commander received an order -- the commander, Ostoja Stanisic received the order from the brigade that we should take over the forward command post of the battalion. While we were carrying out preparations and mobilising the troops, the few of them who were available from the battalion, to take control of the forward command post, two or three soldiers and a commander, perhaps a platoon commander, from the 4th Company arrived in the meantime and they requested that one of the command members should come over to the company which was up in Parlog where there was fierce fighting on the following day, that he should be in the company of the soldiers from this company because there was fear among the troops and our presence was supposed to provide calm and a certain sense of security among the troops. Around 1.00 or 2.00 in the morning, we came to the forward command post of Petrovo Strana, it was the 6th Infantry Battalion, our battalion from Petkovci, the commander and myself and some members of the command itself, I cannot remember all the people who were there at the moment. The commander Ostoja Stanisic remained at the forward command post and he sent me to the left wing, that is to say, to the 4th Company positions, together with the commander or two or three soldiers from this company so that I would link up the line and remain with them and provide a sense of security, because we expected fierce fighting to begin in the early morning on the 16th of July, considering that we were informed, as far as I remember, that the Muslim forces were close by behind the backs of our 4th Battalion and had set some of our equipment on fire, had killed some troops and had made a big fire which caused additional disturbance among the members of our battalion. Therefore, we took these positions up there so that in the morning we would be ready when the expected fierce enemy attack came from the direction of Nezuk and Zaseok from the -- from ahead of us. And from behind us, on the other hand, there would also be an attack of the Muslim Army which was trying to break through from the direction of Srebrenica. So the situation was really difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said a moment ago from Nezuk and from Zaseok. Was that a place called Zaseok or a group of hamlets? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the area in front of our line of defence there were two places. One was called Zaseok and the other was called Nezuk, so two villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have it on the record. You said a moment ago that you had been informed, you didn't say by whom, whether by the brigade or other battalions, that in your rear there were -- there was equipment torched, that a number of soldiers had been killed and that you could see fire burning. Could you tell us about a bit more about this, do you know what had been set on fire, what kind of equipment or pieces of armament and so on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, perhaps you misunderstood or maybe I misspoke. My commander probably received information from those who could observe this. Maybe it was by the 4th Battalion or the Boskovic Battalion, I don't know. But it boils down to this: They said that they had seen the fire up there and that a number of soldiers had been killed and that some equipment was destroyed. We could not observe that portion. We did not have a line of visibility. Now, had we been on the line at the time, perhaps we could have seen this but we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that's all I wanted because -- for the purposes of the record. Now, could you please tell us, did such combat extend to the 16th? So was there combat in the sector covered by your battalion? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, on the 16th of July in early -- early in the morning I was at the forward command post. Or rather, he had ordered me to go to the 4th Company to the left flank of our battalion and to be in the trench there where we could maintain communication, radio communication. That's where I went early in the morning. And in the early morning hours, let's say about 4.00 or 5.00, because it was summertime, I could judge, fierce combat began. And from Nezuk and Zaseok and maybe even Medjedja, artillery mortar fire was opened on our positions, and on the other side, our neighbouring battalion was under a fierce attack by Muslim forces. We couldn't see this but we could hear it -- or rather, in the direction of the 4th Battalion, which was to the left of our forces. However, it was foggy, we couldn't really see much. We could just hear a lot of noise and we could hear voices saying, you know, Kill them, massacre them, slit their throats and so on. But we couldn't really see anything because it was -- there was dense fog and -- but we received a lot of fire, perhaps hundreds of thousands of shells fell on our positions on that day and many people were wounded and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Something was omitted in the transcript, the portions where you said about what these people who were attacking were shouting and from what positions they came and what direction they were going to. Now, please always indicate what direction the attacks came from. You said they were coming from the front line, we know that's in Nezuk, but you should also say from the forces that were being established in Srebrenica. Coming from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what do you want to know from the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question first was which forces attacked the neighbouring battalion, and the witness mentioned this, but it did not -- it was not recorded in the transcript. And second, which forces were attacking from the direction of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our defence line, the defence line of the 6th Battalion, or rather, the entire line was under artillery fire from Nezuk, Zaseok, and Medjedja. And the 4th Battalion, which was to our left, and their positions were on a hill, were also under mortar fire and they were attacked from the rear by the Muslim forces that were moving from the direction of Srebrenica towards them, trying to break through.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us please what kind of -- how did this -- how did the troops that were advancing from Srebrenica and coming behind your lines, how did they behave, what did they yell out, what was characteristic of their conduct? The reason I'm asking this is that what -- your earlier words were not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. The 4th Battalion, which was to the left of our 6th Battalion, or rather, the command, was in Baljkovica which was in a valley, and on that morning it was covered in fog. We couldn't see anything. When early in the morning the combat operations began, we could only hear the shouting and the clamour and a lot of shooting. "Allahu Akbar," and "Kill them," and "Slaughter them," and that's all we could hear. We couldn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us now, did you also hear fire, did you hear artillery fire or infantry fire? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was both artillery and infantry fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us how did all this end on the 15th and did it continue on the 16th? So how did the combat go on? How did it -- and how long did it go on for? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, what I've just talked about was early in the morning on the 16th of July in 1995, so this began early in the morning at dawn both infantry and artillery fire was opened, and it went on for perhaps up until the afternoon. And as I've already said, I had losses in the 4th Company and later on, around 1.30, I too was wounded and taken to the Zvornik hospital. Now, when the combat ended on that day and what happened after my wounding, I really can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's exactly what I wanted to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should realise we are just past the time for the first break. We must have the first break now and we will resume at 11.00. The Court Officer will assist you during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you said -- actually, not that you said but it's a fact that you were wounded on the 16th, I don't want to ask you about that anymore because then it would be second-hand information. I just want to ask you about things that you yourself can confirm. During your cross-examination here on page 1337, the Prosecutor asked you whether you questioned prisoners and whether that was among your tasks, and you said that you considered it your duty to sends Muslim prisoners to the brigade. Can you please tell us which year that was and did that refer to the combat actions at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This didn't relate to the July 1995 combat actions. This was in 1994, when a Muslim soldier was arrested and when he was brought to the command and then when he was sent to the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, for the record, I think you were referring to page 13307 instead of 1337; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are correct, Your Honour. I made the error. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Later during the examination on page 14, they insisted whether you were in charge of interrogating witnesses during the six months that you were performing these duties. And you say here for the transcript during those six months while you were on duty as assistant commander for security, you interrogated any of the prisoners other than this one Muslim who was captured in 1994, as you described. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now please tell us for the transcript whether your role during those six months when you were assistant commander for security was an advisory or a command type of function? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I carried out different duties in the battalion ranging from assistant commander for security, assistant commander for morale and finally as deputy commander for the 6th Battalion. These duties that I carried out, I carried them out the way I thought they should be carried out and I was listening to the orders of my commander, which is what I said before. In my view, these were separate concrete functions, they were not of an advisory nature at any point in time but were pursuant to the rules of command and this is how we worked. And my commander would know that quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is why I asked you in the period while you were carrying out the duty ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't realise that. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think I know why Mr. Vanderpuye is on his feet. Mr. Tolimir on page 36 of the transcript today referred to page 13 of the transcript today, not on page 1337 from the Popovic case, so I'm making that correction for the transcript. He wanted to refer to actually pages 13 and 14 of today's transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have it clear on the record. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked you, sir, whether during the six months while you were assistant for security, were you able to issue orders, and if so, to whom did you issue orders as assistant commander for security, or was it the case that during that time you were carrying out some other function? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was not able to issue any orders. I was only receiving orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time were you able to make any suggestions or proposals or provide advice about how things should be done to somebody who would perhaps request your advice? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From what I can recall of my work, no advice was sought from me. None of the commanders asked for advice from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 13308 -- I am sorry, I've got the wrong page. I apologise to the interpreters. During the Popovic testimony on page 13001 [as interpreted], lines 1 and 2, you said that Ostoja Stanisic took 20 or 30 soldiers to the brigade because those soldiers were supposed to go to Snagovo. On the basis of what you've said, my question is, are you able to tell us why these soldiers were needed in Snagovo and what was the point of sending them to that sector? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What I know is that my commander, on the 14th of July, took a platoon, I don't know exactly how many men that was, one platoon of soldiers to the Zvornik Brigade because he was asked to bring them so that they could be sent to Snagovo because it was probably assessed that the Muslim forces moving from the direction of Srebrenica could endanger the town of Zvornik itself and the Serb-inhabited settlements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one small correction. On page 38, line 15, the correct transcript reference would be 13301. This is the Popovic transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Gajic. Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, since you were wounded, did you perhaps hear later how the fighting ended in the area where you were wounded and in the neighbouring section of the battalion that was there? How did that fighting end? What was the outcome? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since I was wounded on the 16th of July between 1.00 and 2.00 p.m. and taken to the hospital, there were visits. There were many wounded in the hospital including myself, so these wounded people received many visits, and what I heard was that the fighting that day was fierce, it went on for hours in the afternoon. And then at the end of that day it all ended with the Muslim forces passing across our lines where that battalion was and that everything that was in front of them they killed, they burned, and they went to the Muslim territory to the village of Nezuk more precisely. This is what I heard. I wasn't there, so I wasn't able to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: For the transcript, can you please tell us what Muslim forces these were?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These were Muslim forces that were moving from the direction of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Milosevic, for your answers. Thank you for coming to testify. I wish you a happy stay and good luck in your future work. I have now finished my cross-examination. Mr. President, I would like to thank you as well. I have completed my cross-examination of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your testimony. You are now free to return to your normal activities, and the Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here today and the assistance you were able to provide us and we wish you also a safe journey back. Thank you very much again and you are free now to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, how is the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we have no further witnesses to finish the time that we have remaining in the day. I don't know if there are any housekeeping matters perhaps we can attend to in order to dispose of those matters while we have some available time, I don't think so. But otherwise, as you know, we discharged one witness who we did not anticipate would be able to testify this week in advance of the situation that arose the other day and that's the reason why we don't have anybody at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: As we are not sitting next week, I think this is an accepted situation. We can't -- it would not be very feasible to start with another witness for a few hours before a break of one week. So if there's nothing else to raise or to discuss, we have to adjourn and we will resume on Monday, the 18th of October, in the afternoon, 2.15, in Courtroom III. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 18th day of October, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.15 a.m.,
